newsitem.title: CHINA: China to lift freeze on listing new mutual funds.
newsitem.headline: China to lift freeze on listing new mutual funds.

text.p: Chinese authorities will shortly promulgate new rules governing China's mutual funds, ending a ban on new listings of such funds that has been in effect since 1993, the official Xinhua news agency said on Wednesday.
"The adoption of the new regulation will be a signal that the freeze over the funds market will thaw," Xinhua quoted a magazine published by the State Planning Commission as saying.
Beijing in the early 1990s encouraged the establishment of mutual funds to raise money from individuals for investment mainly in stocks and in real estate during a boom in those two industries.

After listing about 22 such funds in China's two stock exchanges in Shanghai and southern Shenzhen, authorities banned new listings in 1993 after finding that many were poorly managed and loss-making.
About 50 such funds still exist, most run by securities houses and brokerages, but these have not been listed and many have turned their investments towards industry.

Xinhua quoted an unnamed offficial as telling the magazine that the promulgation of the rules would help to standardise the management of funds. The rules would encourage more institutional investors and boost stock markets, he said.

"The long-awaited regulation was designed in keeping with the state's policy of encouraging enterprises to raise capital from the securities market instead of lending solely from the banks," the official was quoted as saying.

The new rules will stipulate that funds in the securities market should be jointly approved and managed by the People's Bank of China -- the central bank -- the Securities Commission under the State Council and the China Securities Regulatory Commission, the securities watchdog, he said.

Only securities houses and trust and investment companies were allowed to apply to establish such funds and each fund would be required to raise at least 1.0 million yuan ($120,000) before listing, he was quoted as saying. Each fund must invest no less than 20 percent of its capital in treasury bonds and combined investments in stocks and bonds must be at least 60 percent, he said.
The rules had been under discussion since 1992 and more than 10 revisions had been made so far, Xinhua said, without giving a precise date for the publication of the new rules.
China would delay drafting of a regulation on the management of funds that are invested in industry to try to cool the development of such funds, it quoted the magazine as saying.
